extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kantian aesthetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for making and evaluating pure aesthetic judgements about the Beautiful and the Sublime, especially in nature, including their grounding, affective character, and claims to universality and autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful = pleases in the mere judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is what pleases in the mere judgement (and therefore not by the medium of sensation in accordance with a concept of the Understanding). It must please apart from all interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize disinterested pleasure: beauty's claim to satisfaction must not rest on sensory gratification or a concept — it pleases 'in the mere judgement'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime = pleases through opposition to sensible interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is what pleases immediately through its opposition to the interest of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the Sublime as a pleasure that arises when an object opposes sensible interest, provoking an idea-related response rather than sensory gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different subjective grounds for Beautiful and Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Both are referred to subjective grounds: in the one case to grounds of sensibility (the Beautiful, favoring contemplative Understanding); in the other case in opposition to sensibility, but on behalf of the purposes of practical Reason (the Sublime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, locate whether the judgement's ground is sensibility (beautiful) or a moral/practical idea opposing sensibility (sublime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful prepares disinterested love; Sublime prepares esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful prepares us to love disinterestedly something, even nature itself; the Sublime prepares us to esteem something highly even in opposition to our own (sensible) interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the resulting attitude: beauty tends toward affectionate, disinterested attraction; the sublime toward respect or esteem that can oppose sensible interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic purposiveness = purposiveness without purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical purposiveness is the conformity to law of the Judgement in its freedom (purposiveness without a concept of a purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge forms by whether they appear purposive for our cognition/apprehension without implying an objective teleological purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity requirement: avoid teleological or sensuous bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure aesthetical judgements must not be based on concepts of purpose (teleological judgements) nor on mere sensations; examples of beauty or sublimity must be free from such contaminating concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving examples or judging, avoid bringing in knowledge that imputes purposes (e.g., thinking of stars as suns for inhabitants) or relying on sensory gratification; treat the object as it strikes the eye alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime arises from the mind's sense of unattainability of Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is an object (of nature) the representation of which determines the mind to think the unattainability of nature regarded as a presentation of Ideas. The Imagination strains to make the senses adequate to Reason's Idea, and the feeling of this unattainability is the presentation of subjective purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accounts of the sublime by whether the imagination is 'strained' toward an Idea or the supersensible, producing the sense of inadequacy/unattainability that grounds the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction valence: Sublime negative vs Beautiful positive
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the Sublime of nature is then only negative (whilst that in the Beautiful is positive); viz. a feeling that the Imagination is depriving itself of its freedom, while it is purposively determined according to a different law from that of its empirical employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether the aesthetic pleasure is experienced as an affirmative, pleasant harmony (beautiful) or as a negative, limiting yet elevating feeling (sublime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime presupposes a moral-like disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A feeling for the Sublime in nature cannot well be thought without combining therewith a mental disposition which is akin to the Moral; the judgement is based upon a feeling of the mind’s destination which surpasses sensibility (the moral feeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the subject's disposition implicates moral ideas or a sense of the supersensible; if not, the 'sublime' response may be impure or merely sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as instrument of Reason in the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: In aesthetical judgements upon the Sublime this dominion (of Reason over Sensibility) is represented as exercised by the Imagination, regarded as an instrument of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing sublime experiences, show how imaginative activity manifests Reason's influence, rather than mere sensory association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleological/rational additions when calling something sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: To call the sight of the starry heaven sublime, we must not place at the basis of our judgement concepts of worlds inhabited by rational beings; likewise for the ocean, we must regard it merely by what strikes the eye and not by teleological conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only the immediate sensible presentation for pure aesthetic judgement; exclude explanatory stories or teleological interpretations when asserting sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual beauty/sublimity differ from aesthetic modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual beauty or sublimity are not quite accurate expressions because beauty and sublimity are aesthetical modes of representation, which would not be found in us at all if we were pure intelligences. Intellectual (moral) good aesthetically judged must be represented as sublime rather than beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish strictly aesthetic (sense-based) reactions from intellectual/moral satisfactions; represent moral/intellectual goods as sublime (evoking respect) rather than beautiful (evoking love).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthusiasm and apatheia in aesthetic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of the Good conjoined with affection is called enthusiasm and is aesthetically sublime to an extent; but the absence of affection (apatheia), following unalterable principles, is sublime in a preferable way because it has satisfaction of pure Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether affective excess (enthusiasm) or principled dispassion (apatheia) better realizes the noble sublime; beware that fanaticism (unbridled imagination) is incompatible with the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish strenuous vs languid affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Every affection of the STRENUOUS kind (that excites the consciousness of our power to overcome every obstacle) is aesthetically sublime (e.g., wrath, despair of indignation). Affections of the LANGUID kind (which make the very effort of resistance an object of pain) have nothing noble and may be reckoned under the sensuously beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify emotions: robust, overcoming affections count toward sublimity; languid, weakening affections toward sensuous beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of sentimentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tender emotions when they rise to the height of affections are worthless; the propensity to them is called sentimentality. Romances, lacrymose plays, shallow moral precepts that make the heart languid are not compatible with what is beautiful or sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sentimentalism as an aesthetic vice: excessive tender emotion that weakens moral strength undermines genuine beauty or sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime must produce a mood of strength and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime must leave a mental mood which has influence upon the mind’s consciousness of its strength, and its resolution in reference to that which involves pure intellectual purposiveness; otherwise the emotions belong only to motion for enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge sublime effects by their lasting influence on conviction, strength, or resolution, not merely by transient excitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as style of the Sublime and Morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity (purposiveness without art) is as it were the style of Nature in the sublime, and so also of Morality which is a second (supersensible) nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value simplicity (artlessness that nevertheless appears purposive) as characteristic of true sublimity and moral grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability/universal claim of aesthetic judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the Beautiful is distinguishable by its universal communicability; the judgement of taste determines its object in respect of satisfaction with an accompanying claim for the assent of every one, just as if it were objective ('this flower is beautiful' claims to satisfy everyone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting beauty, be prepared to make a universal claim (communicability) even though it is not a cognitive universality — evaluate how the object 'accommodates itself to our mode of apprehension.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of taste: a priori and independent judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste should be pronounced a priori, and not be a mere imitation of others; it claims autonomy — the subject shall judge by himself without needing to consult the judgement of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a taste-judgement is genuinely autonomous (formed without deference to public opinion) rather than heteronomous or merely imitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two logical peculiarities of judgements of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: First, there is its a priori universal validity, which is not a logical universality in accordance with concepts, but the universality of a singular judgement. Secondly, it has a necessity (resting on a priori grounds) which, however, does not depend on any a priori grounds of proof that could exact assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the paradoxical character: taste-judgements claim necessary, universal validity despite not being grounded in concepts or provable by conceptual argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste not determinable by grounds of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is not determinable by grounds of proof; if a man does not find something beautiful, a hundred voices praising it will not force his inmost agreement — taste is not subject to proof like cognitive judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating aesthetic judgement as if it could be established by argument or evidence in the same way as cognitive claims; evaluate authenticity of taste rather than its provability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of exemplars and following vs imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although taste claims autonomy, examples of exemplary authors or works (classics) serve as guidance: following (drawing from same sources) is appropriate to cultivate taste, whereas mere imitation or heteronomy is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage use of exemplars to train taste while preserving autonomy; distinguish healthy following (learning sources) from slavish imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction requirement for judgements of taste about beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim of an aesthetical judgement to universal validity for every subject requires, as a judgement resting on some a priori principle, a Deduction (legitimising of its pretensions) in addition to its Exposition; this is needed particularly for judgements of taste about the Beautiful in Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, provide a priori justification (deduction) for claims of universal validity in taste, especially when asserting beauty in natural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty appears as accommodation to our mode of apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste consists in calling a thing beautiful because of that characteristic in respect of which it accommodates itself to our mode of apprehension; beauty seems to be regarded as a property of the object that fits our cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the object's form exemplifies a fit or harmony with our cognitive faculties of apprehension — beauty is the object's accommodation to those faculties, not mere subjective whim.
